options: highest at the base of the lung
highest at the apex of the lung

questions.explanation: this reserve is available during exercise.

questions.explanation: about 70%.

questions.stem: The dorsal respiratory group:
options: sets the basic rhythm through the phrenic and intercostal nerves and integrates sensory input

questions.stem: Overstimulation of the pneumotaxic center would cause breathing that is:
questions.explanation: it shortens inspiration.

questions.stem: The Hering-Breuer (inflation) reflex is triggered by:
options: stretch receptors sensing overinflation of the lungs

questions.stem: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond mainly to:
options: increased H+ in cerebrospinal fluid caused by rising PCO2

questions.stem: Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the:

automatically start breathing again when CO2 rises high enough

A normal adult resting respiratory rate is:

questions.stem: Deep, labored, regular breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis (metabolic acidosis) is:
Cycles of gradually deeper then shallower breaths separated by apnea (crescendo-decrescendo), seen in heart failure, is:

Prolonged, gasping inspirations with a pause before a short exhalation, seen with damage to the upper pons, is:
Difficulty breathing when lying flat, common in heart failure, is:
Labored, uncomfortable breathing ("air hunger") is:
A blood CO2 level below normal is:
questions.explanation: hyperventilation causes it, which raises pH (respiratory alkalosis).

questions.stem: Rapid, shallow breathing from anxiety lowers blood CO2. The result is:
questions.explanation: symptoms include tingling, dizziness and muscle spasms (tetany).

questions.stem: Respiratory failure (inadequate ventilation) causes:
options: pH to fall and CO2 to rise
pH to rise and CO2 to rise
pH to rise and CO2 to fall

questions.explanation: alveolar ventilation is (TV − dead space) × rate.

questions.stem: An FEV1/FVC ratio below about ___ indicates obstructive lung disease.
Lung compliance is:
options: the force needed to move air through the airways
how easily the lungs stretch: change in volume ÷ change in pressure
the volume of the lungs at rest

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis causes:
options: decreased compliance and decreased vital capacity

questions.stem: Emphysema causes compliance to:
options: increase, because elastic fibers are destroyed
questions.explanation: recoil is lost, so air is trapped and exhaling is hard.

questions.stem: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema because:
options: elastase from neutrophils is left unchecked and destroys alveolar walls

questions.stem: Smoking damages the respiratory tract mainly by:
options: paralyzing and destroying cilia and increasing mucus

questions.stem: Select ALL obstructive lung diseases:
Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as a productive cough for:
options: 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years

questions.stem: Asthma symptoms are mainly caused by inflammation and constriction of the:

Tuberculosis is caused by:
questions.explanation: infected macrophages are walled off in granulomas (tubercles).

questions.stem: The drug commonly used to treat tuberculosis is:
questions.explanation: combined with rifampin and others for months.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old has fever, cough and a hazy right lower lobe on x-ray. The best vaccine to have prevented this is the:
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: Coughing up green mucus with fever and shortness of breath most strongly suggests:

questions.explanation: the most common mutation is ΔF508.

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in a premature baby is treated mainly with:
questions.explanation: giving the mother corticosteroids before delivery speeds the baby's surfactant production.

questions.stem: Sharp chest pain that worsens with each breath, caused by inflamed pleura, is:
Air in the pleural space that collapses the lung is:
questions.explanation: atelectasis is the collapse; pneumothorax is the air.

questions.stem: Which is most likely to cause a collapsed lung?
A blood clot that travels to and blocks a pulmonary artery is a:
questions.explanation: it increases alveolar dead space (ventilated but not perfused).

questions.stem: Fluid build-up in the alveoli, often from left heart failure, is:
questions.explanation: patients may cough up pink, frothy sputum; treated with diuretics such as furosemide.

questions.stem: Lung disease caused by inhaling mineral dust (coal, silica, asbestos) is called:
Long-term asbestos exposure is linked to:
The most common type of lung cancer overall is:
Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by:
options: the brain failing to send signals to breathe
repeated collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep
questions.explanation: risk factors include obesity; it is diagnosed with a polysomnogram (sleep study) and treated with CPAP.

questions.stem: The common cold, inflammation of the nasal mucosa, is:
Inflammation of the vocal folds causing hoarseness is:
Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the:

options: air is forced out through the nose and the uvula is depressed

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a non-respiratory air movement?
Which is NOT a function of the respiratory system?
When rising quickly to high altitude, the first thing that drives faster breathing is:
options: hypoxic stimulation of carotid body chemoreceptors

questions.stem: Over weeks at high altitude, which change helps the body adapt?
options: increased erythropoietin and red blood cell count

questions.stem: Rapid ascent to high altitude can cause high-altitude pulmonary edema because:
options: hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels, raising pressure and pushing fluid into alveoli

questions.stem: Decompression sickness ("the bends") is explained by:
Which would NOT normally be treated with 100% oxygen?
questions.explanation: in an emphysema patient who retains CO2, high-flow oxygen must also be used with caution.

questions.stem: Which describes aging of the respiratory system?
options: costal cartilage becomes stiffer and elastic tissue decreases

questions.stem: Exercise training improves breathing mainly by:
options: strengthening the diaphragm and intercostal muscles

questions.stem: In the Weibel model of the airways, gas exchange begins at about generation:
questions.explanation: generations 0–16 are conducting; 17–23 are the respiratory zone.

questions.stem: In a patient whose lung compliance is half normal, with normal tidal volume and rate:
options: the total work of breathing increases
alveolar pressure is positive at end-inspiration
questions.explanation: pleural pressure must become more negative to inflate stiff lungs.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a function of the respiratory system?
options: helping return venous blood and lymph to the heart through pressure changes in the chest
questions.explanation: breathing's pressure changes do aid venous and lymph return (the "respiratory pump").

questions.stem: The olfactory epithelium, which detects smells, is located:
options: in the roof of the nasal cavity

questions.stem: The respiratory membrane that gases cross consists of:
options: alveolar epithelium, fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium
questions.explanation: it is only about 0.5 µm thick.

questions.stem: Air flow (F) through the airways depends on the pressure gradient and resistance (F = ΔP/R). The factor that most changes airway resistance is:
questions.explanation: resistance rises sharply as radius falls, which is why bronchoconstriction in asthma is so serious.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation (epinephrine) affects the bronchioles by causing:
questions.explanation: parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation causes bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: A spirogram trace shows each quiet breath rising and falling by about 0.5 L. This volume is the:
On a spirogram, the largest single excursion from a maximal inhalation to a maximal exhalation is the:
questions.explanation: TLC cannot be read directly because residual volume never leaves the lungs.

questions.stem: On a forced-exhalation spirogram (volume vs time), an obstructive disease shows:
options: a steep curve that reaches its plateau within about 1 second
a slowly rising curve that takes many seconds to reach a plateau, with a low FEV1
a small, quick curve with a high FEV1/FVC
questions.explanation: a restrictive disease shows a small but fast curve.

questions.stem: During strenuous exercise, minute ventilation can rise from about 6 L/min to more than:
questions.explanation: both tidal volume and rate increase.

questions.stem: At the start of exercise, breathing rises abruptly within seconds, before blood gases change. This is mainly due to:
options: neural input from the motor cortex and from proprioceptors in moving muscles and joints
questions.explanation: arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay nearly normal during moderate exercise.

questions.stem: During exercise, which change increases O2 unloading to working muscle?
options: higher CO2, H+ and temperature, shifting the curve right

questions.stem: Long-term endurance training does NOT:
options: strengthen the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
increase the number of alveoli in an adult
increase capillary density in skeletal muscle

questions.stem: Erythropoietin (EPO), which increases red blood cell production at high altitude, is released mainly by the:
Over days at high altitude, the kidneys excrete more bicarbonate. This:
options: corrects the respiratory alkalosis caused by hyperventilation
questions.explanation: acetazolamide speeds this and helps prevent altitude sickness.

questions.stem: People native to high altitudes (such as in the Andes) typically have:
options: smaller chests and fewer red blood cells
larger lung volumes and higher hematocrit

questions.stem: The best single treatment for acute mountain sickness that is worsening is:
COPD includes mainly:
The leading cause of COPD is:
questions.explanation: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic cause.

questions.stem: A "pink puffer" is a COPD patient with mainly:
questions.explanation: "blue bloaters" have mainly chronic bronchitis, with cyanosis and edema.

questions.stem: Which COPD patient is most likely to have a barrel chest from air trapping?
Status asthmaticus is:
options: a severe asthma attack that does not respond to usual bronchodilators
questions.explanation: it is a medical emergency.

questions.stem: An asthma attack has an early phase driven by mast-cell histamine and a late phase (hours later) driven by:
questions.explanation: this is why inhaled steroids are used for long-term control.

questions.stem: Pneumonia acquired in a hospital or on a ventilator is most often caused by:
options: gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus aureus

questions.stem: On a chest x-ray, pneumonia of one whole lobe appears as:
questions.explanation: alveoli are filled with fluid, pus and cells.

questions.stem: Central sleep apnea differs from obstructive sleep apnea because in central apnea:
options: the brain fails to send signals to the breathing muscles
questions.explanation: it is linked to heart failure, stroke and opioid use.

questions.stem: A sleep study counts pauses in breathing per hour to give the:
questions.explanation: an AHI of 30 or more per hour is severe.

questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis patients often have poor growth because:
options: thick mucus blocks pancreatic ducts, so digestive enzymes cannot reach the intestine
questions.explanation: they take pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals.

questions.stem: Most men with cystic fibrosis are infertile because:
options: the vas deferens is blocked or absent

questions.stem: CFTR modulator drugs (such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) work by:
options: helping the faulty CFTR channel fold correctly and open

questions.stem: The mucociliary escalator moves mucus up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out.
Inhalation is active and quiet exhalation is passive.
Type I pneumocytes make surfactant and type II pneumocytes carry out gas exchange.
questions.explanation: type II make surfactant; type I form the thin exchange surface.

questions.stem: Oxygen binds the central magnesium atom of heme.
questions.explanation: it binds iron (Fe2+).

questions.stem: The normal pH range of arterial blood is 7.35–7.45.
Hyperventilation makes the blood more acidic.
questions.explanation: it removes CO2 and makes blood more alkaline.

questions.stem: Bronchioles have cartilage rings like the trachea.
questions.explanation: bronchioles have no cartilage.

questions.stem: The left main bronchus is shorter and more vertical than the right.
questions.explanation: the right is shorter, wider and more vertical.

questions.stem: O2 is more soluble in water than CO2.
questions.explanation: CO2 is about 20 times more soluble.

questions.stem: An increase in body temperature decreases gas solubility and shifts the O2 curve to the right.
The PO2 of tissue cells is higher than that of arterial blood.
questions.explanation: it is lower, so O2 diffuses into the tissues.

questions.stem: Residual volume can be measured with a simple spirometer.
questions.explanation: it needs helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography.

questions.stem: Pneumonia is always caused by a virus.
questions.explanation: it can be bacterial, viral or fungal; bacteria (especially S. pneumoniae) are common causes.

questions.stem: Tuberculosis is a viral disease.
questions.explanation: it is bacterial.

questions.stem: Obesity is a common cause of restrictive lung physiology.
Exercise decreases the amount of anatomical dead space.
questions.explanation: anatomical dead space stays about the same; deeper breaths make it a smaller fraction of each breath.

questions.stem: The lungs are compartmentalized, so damage to one lobe does not necessarily affect the others.
Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid sinus and the atria.
questions.explanation: they are in the carotid and aortic bodies.

questions.stem: You can consciously override breathing for a short time using the cerebral cortex.
questions.explanation: not the cerebellum.

questions.stem: The trachea is reinforced by hyaline cartilage.
Hering-Breuer reflex receptors are in the medulla.
questions.explanation: they are stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles.

questions.stem: Fetal hemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin.
The pleural cavity is a potential space, normally with almost no room in it.
The alveoli provide about 70 square meters of surface area for gas exchange.
The common cold (acute rhinitis) has no cure.
questions.explanation: treatment is supportive.

questions.stem: A smoker's FVC is 5.02 L and FEV1 is 2.61 L. Calculate FEV1/FVC and state whether this pattern is obstructive or restrictive.

questions.answer_text: A: 50%, obstructive. B: 86%, restrictive pattern (low FVC with normal or high ratio; confirm with low TLC).

questions.stem: A woman's FVC is 40% of predicted, FEV1/FVC is 61%, and TLC is 52% of predicted. Her FVC falls further when she lies down. Classify her disease. Which muscle is likely weak?
questions.answer_text: Restrictive (TLC low). A large drop in FVC when supine points to diaphragm weakness.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old non-smoker exposed to asbestos has FVC 102% of predicted, FEV1/FVC 73%, TLC 113% of predicted, and no change after a bronchodilator. Interpret.
questions.answer_text: Normal spirometry: no airflow obstruction, no restriction (TLC normal to high), no significant bronchodilator response; DLCO only mildly low. Keep monitoring for asbestos-related disease.

questions.stem: A bronchodilator raises a patient's FEV1 by 15% and 300 mL. This suggests:
questions.answer_text: reversible airway obstruction, typical of asthma (a significant response is ≥ 12% and ≥ 200 mL).

questions.stem: Describe how a flow-volume loop looks in obstructive disease and in restrictive disease compared with a healthy loop.
questions.answer_text: Obstructive: lower peak flow, "scooped" (concave) expiratory limb, loop shifted toward larger volumes. Restrictive: small, narrow loop of near-normal shape shifted toward smaller volumes.

questions.stem: Define FEV1 and FVC. How does the FEV1/FVC ratio change in obstructive vs restrictive disease?
questions.answer_text: FEV1: volume forcibly exhaled in the first second. FVC: total volume forcibly exhaled after a maximal breath in. Obstructive: ratio falls (< 70%). Restrictive: ratio normal or high.

A diver uses a snorkel that adds 300 mL of dead space. With TV 500 mL, anatomical dead space 150 mL and rate 12/min, what is the new alveolar ventilation?

questions.stem: Two patients' spirograms: Patient X has TLC 8.0 L, RV 3.5 L, VC 4.5 L. Patient Y has TLC 3.8 L, RV 1.0 L, VC 2.8 L. Classify each pattern and name a disease that fits.

questions.explanation: emphysema/COPD. Y: restrictive (low TLC and VC) — pulmonary fibrosis or obesity.

questions.stem: During exercise, an athlete's tidal volume rises from 0.5 L to 2.5 L and rate from 12 to 40 breaths/min. Dead space is 0.15 L. Calculate minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation at rest and during exercise.
questions.answer_text: Rest: VE = 6 L/min; VA = (0.5 − 0.15) × 12 = 4.2 L/min. Exercise: VE = 100 L/min; VA = (2.5 − 0.15) × 40 = 94 L/min.

questions.stem: At sea level hemoglobin is 98% saturated; at high altitude it is 85%. If a person has 150 g/L hemoglobin and each gram carries 1.34 mL O2 when saturated, calculate O2 carried per liter of blood in each case.

Read an oxygen dissociation curve: arterial blood at PO2 100 mmHg is 98% saturated; venous blood at 40 mmHg is 75% saturated. What percentage of the O2 was unloaded to the tissues? During exercise, muscle PO2 falls to 20 mmHg (35% saturated). What percentage is unloaded now?
questions.answer_text: Rest: 98 − 75 = 23 percentage points (about 23% of the O2). Exercise: 98 − 35 = 63 percentage points (about 64% of the O2).

questions.stem: The P50 is the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (normally about 27 mmHg). If a person's P50 rises to 32 mmHg, which way has the curve shifted, and what might cause it?
questions.answer_text: To the right (lower affinity). Causes: exercise, fever, acidosis, high CO2, more 2,3-BPG (altitude).

questions.stem: Name the three ways CO2 is carried in blood, with approximate percentages. Explain the roles of carbonic anhydrase and the chloride shift.
questions.answer_text: ~70% as bicarbonate, ~20–23% as carbaminohemoglobin, ~7–10% dissolved. Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells rapidly converts CO2 + H2O to H2CO3, which splits into H+ and HCO3−. HCO3− leaves the cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift), keeping the gradient so more CO2 can load.

questions.stem: CO2 is a neutral molecule. Explain, with an equation, how rising CO2 lowers blood pH.
questions.answer_text: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. More CO2 drives the reaction right, raising H+ and lowering pH (respiratory acidosis).

questions.stem: A person lacks carbonic anhydrase. Predict what happens to CO2 transport and blood pH.
questions.answer_text: CO2 and carbonic acid cannot interconvert quickly, so far less CO2 is carried as bicarbonate. CO2 builds up in tissues and blood, lowering pH (acidosis).

questions.stem: Explain why hemoglobin's sigmoidal curve is useful. Include positive cooperativity and what happens at about 40 mmHg.
questions.answer_text: Binding of the first O2 changes hemoglobin's shape and raises affinity for the next O2 (positive cooperativity). In the lungs (~100 mmHg) the flat top keeps hemoglobin nearly 100% saturated even if PO2 drops a little. At tissue PO2 (~40 mmHg) the curve is steep, so a small drop in PO2 releases a lot of O2.

questions.stem: Why does fetal hemoglobin's curve lie to the left of adult hemoglobin's? Why is this useful? What disease can be treated by inducing HbF?
questions.answer_text: HbF has 2 alpha and 2 gamma chains; gamma chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly, so HbF has higher O2 affinity. This pulls O2 from maternal blood across the placenta. Sickle cell disease: hydroxyurea raises HbF, which prevents sickling.

questions.stem: How does the myoglobin dissociation curve differ in shape from hemoglobin's, and why?
questions.answer_text: Myoglobin's curve is hyperbolic and left-shifted because it has one heme and no cooperative binding. It stores O2 in muscle and releases it only at very low PO2.

questions.stem: Define surfactant generally. Explain why pulmonary surfactant is important, using the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r).
questions.answer_text: A surfactant lowers the surface tension of water. Without it, surface tension would make small alveoli (small r, high pressure) collapse and empty into larger ones. Surfactant lowers tension more in small alveoli, keeping all alveoli open and reducing the work of breathing.

questions.stem: Donald coughs up thick mucus and has high chloride in his sweat. Name the disease, how it is inherited and the affected protein. Explain why his mucus is thick and why the pH of his small intestine is lower than normal.
questions.answer_text: Cystic fibrosis; autosomal recessive; CFTR chloride channel. Without Cl− secretion, Na+ and water are pulled out of the airway, leaving dehydrated, sticky mucus. Pancreatic duct cells need CFTR to secrete bicarbonate, so less HCO3− reaches the duodenum and its pH drops; thick secretions also block the ducts.

questions.stem: A boy born in 2000 fails to gain weight, has greasy, foul-smelling stools and a productive cough by 4 months. Name the disease, the most common mutation, and one bacterium he is especially prone to.
questions.answer_text: Cystic fibrosis; ΔF508 in CFTR; Pseudomonas aeruginosa (also Staphylococcus aureus).

questions.stem: How is cystic fibrosis diagnosed and treated? Is there a cure?
questions.answer_text: Newborn screening (high immunoreactive trypsinogen), sweat chloride test, genetic testing. Treatment: airway clearance, mucolytics, antibiotics, bronchodilators, pancreatic enzymes, CFTR modulators. No cure; lung transplant in severe cases.

questions.stem: A stab wound causes a collapsed left lung. Using Palv, Pip and Ptp, explain why it collapsed. Why did the right lung not collapse? Name two risk factors for a spontaneous pneumothorax.
questions.answer_text: Air enters the pleural space, so Pip rises to atmospheric pressure. Ptp (Palv − Pip) falls to 0, so nothing holds the lung open and elastic recoil collapses it. Each lung has its own pleural cavity. Risk factors: tall, thin young male; smoking; COPD or CF; Marfan syndrome.

questions.stem: Left heart failure causes blood to back up in the pulmonary circulation. Explain how this causes pulmonary edema. Give two reasons PO2 falls more than PCO2 rises when diffusion is impaired.
questions.answer_text: Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium and alveoli, thickening the diffusion barrier. (1) CO2 is about 20× more soluble and diffuses faster. (2) Extra ventilation easily blows off CO2 but cannot add much O2 to blood leaving well-ventilated alveoli (hemoglobin is already near saturation).

questions.stem: Jeffrey, an obese heavy smoker with heart disease, suddenly becomes short of breath, wheezes and coughs up pink, frothy sputum. Name the condition and whether it is acute or chronic. Give two immediate treatments and two tests.
questions.answer_text: Acute pulmonary edema (cardiogenic). Treatment: sit upright, oxygen, diuretic (furosemide), nitrates/positive-pressure ventilation. Tests: chest x-ray, echocardiogram, BNP blood test, ECG, arterial blood gas.

questions.stem: Players collapsed during a game at 7,400 ft. Explain the effect of altitude on O2 loading and unloading, and name two ways the body adapts over weeks.
questions.answer_text: Lower atmospheric PO2 lowers alveolar PO2, so less O2 loads onto hemoglobin and delivery to muscles falls. Adaptations: faster/deeper breathing, more EPO and red cells, more 2,3-BPG, more capillaries and mitochondria.

questions.stem: Climbers new to high altitude breathe much faster. Will this cause acidosis or alkalosis? Explain using the bicarbonate equation. What are the two dangerous forms of altitude sickness?
questions.answer_text: Respiratory alkalosis: rapid breathing removes CO2, the equation shifts left, H+ falls and pH rises. Dangerous forms: high-altitude pulmonary edema and high-altitude cerebral edema.

questions.stem: After scuba diving, Jeff boards a plane and develops elbow pain. What is happening, which gas law explains it, and what is the treatment?
questions.answer_text: Decompression sickness: extra N2 dissolved in blood under pressure forms bubbles as pressure drops. Henry's law. Treat with hyperbaric oxygen (recompression).

questions.stem: Randy, a pack-a-day smoker, has worsening shortness of breath. His FEV1/FVC is 52% and his DLCO is low. Name the disease and give the reasoning. Is his residual volume increased or decreased? Name two things you would do to help him.
questions.answer_text: Emphysema: obstructive pattern (ratio < 70%) plus low DLCO from destroyed alveolar surface (chronic bronchitis usually has normal DLCO). RV is increased (air trapping). Help: stop smoking, bronchodilators/inhaled steroids, pulmonary rehab, oxygen, vaccines.

questions.stem: Emphysema: name the main symptom, explain what causes it physiologically, and describe what happens over time.
questions.answer_text: Main symptom: shortness of breath. Destroyed alveolar walls reduce gas-exchange area and elastic recoil, so air is trapped and exhaling is hard. Over time, alveoli merge into large air spaces (bullae), the chest becomes barrel-shaped and breathing work rises.

questions.stem: Overstimulated pneumotaxic center: describe the rate and depth of breathing, whether hypercapnia or hypocapnia results, and whether gas exchange becomes more efficient.
questions.answer_text: Rapid, shallow breathing; hypocapnia; no, a larger share of each small breath is dead space, so alveolar ventilation is less efficient.

questions.stem: Why are the C-rings of the trachea incomplete posteriorly?
questions.answer_text: So the esophagus behind the trachea can bulge forward when a large bolus is swallowed; the trachealis muscle also changes airway diameter for coughing.

questions.stem: Describe what happens during swallowing to keep food out of the airway.
questions.answer_text: The soft palate and uvula rise to close off the nasopharynx; the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds over the glottis; the vocal cords close; breathing briefly stops.

questions.stem: What force must be overcome during inspiration? Why does the lung not collapse at rest?
questions.answer_text: The inward elastic recoil of the lungs (and alveolar surface tension). The negative intrapleural pressure and cohesion of pleural fluid hold the lung against the chest wall, and surfactant reduces surface tension.

questions.stem: What happens to PO2 and PCO2 during voluntary hyperventilation?
questions.answer_text: Alveolar PO2 rises (toward ~120 mmHg) and PCO2 falls (toward ~20 mmHg).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old obese man snores loudly, has morning headaches and is sleepy during the day. Name the likely disorder, its mechanism, how it is diagnosed and treated.
questions.answer_text: Obstructive sleep apnea: repeated collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep. Diagnosed by polysomnogram; treated with CPAP, weight loss, oral appliances or surgery.

questions.stem: In the Weibel airway model, how does the partial pressure of H2O, CO2 and O2 in generation 1 (bronchi) compare with generation 22 (alveolar sacs) after inhalation?
questions.answer_text: H2O: less in generation 1 (accept "same"; air is nearly fully humidified by the trachea); CO2: less in generation 1; O2: greater in generation 1. Fresh air mixes with alveolar gas, so CO2 rises and O2 falls toward the alveoli.

questions.stem: How would a pulmonary embolism and a right-to-left shunt each affect alveolar dead space?
questions.answer_text: Pulmonary embolism increases alveolar dead space (ventilated, not perfused). A shunt does not increase dead space; it is perfused but not ventilated (V/Q = 0).

questions.stem: Compare the effects of a single bout of exercise with long-term training on the respiratory system.
questions.answer_text: Single bout: ventilation rises sharply (deeper and faster breaths) from neural input then chemical fine-tuning; more O2 unloaded (curve shifts right with heat, CO2 and H+); more lung capillaries open, so perfusion and diffusion rise. Training: stronger breathing muscles and higher maximum ventilation; more capillaries and mitochondria in muscle, so muscles extract more O2; lower breathing rate at a given workload; lung volumes and alveoli number change little.

questions.stem: Compare chronic bronchitis and emphysema: what is damaged, the main symptom, typical blood gases and appearance.
questions.answer_text: Chronic bronchitis: inflamed airways, enlarged mucous glands, damaged cilia; productive cough; early hypoxemia and CO2 retention, cyanosis and edema ("blue bloater"). Emphysema: destroyed alveolar walls and lost elastic recoil; shortness of breath; breathes hard to keep gases near normal, thin with barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing ("pink puffer").

questions.stem: Explain why an asthma attack makes it harder to exhale than to inhale.
questions.answer_text: During inhalation, the expanding lungs pull airways open. During exhalation, the pressure around the airways rises and squeezes already narrowed, inflamed, mucus-filled bronchioles shut, trapping air (wheezing on exhalation).

questions.stem: Name three common asthma triggers and two types of asthma medicines (with how each works).
questions.answer_text: Triggers: allergens (pollen, dust mites, pet dander), exercise, cold air, smoke, infections, NSAIDs. Medicines: quick-relief beta-2 agonists (albuterol) relax bronchial smooth muscle; inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation; leukotriene blockers (montelukast) block inflammatory mediators.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old has fever, a cough producing rusty sputum, chest pain on breathing and crackles over one lung. Name the likely diagnosis and organism. Explain why his blood O2 is low.
questions.answer_text: Lobar pneumonia, most likely Streptococcus pneumoniae. Alveoli fill with fluid, pus and cells, so blood flowing past them is not oxygenated (shunt), lowering PaO2.

questions.stem: Why does obstructive sleep apnea raise the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease?
questions.answer_text: Repeated drops in blood O2 and arousals trigger sympathetic surges (high heart rate and blood pressure) many times a night; long-term this raises blood pressure and strains the heart, increasing risk of heart failure, arrhythmia and stroke.

questions.stem: Describe cystic fibrosis at each level: gene, protein, cell, organ and whole person.
questions.answer_text: Gene: mutations in CFTR (chromosome 7), autosomal recessive (ΔF508 most common). Protein: misfolded or nonfunctional chloride channel. Cell: epithelial cells cannot secrete Cl−, so water does not follow and mucus is thick and dehydrated. Organs: lungs (blocked airways, chronic Pseudomonas infections), pancreas (blocked ducts, malabsorption, CF-related diabetes), intestines (meconium ileus), sweat glands (salty sweat), vas deferens. Whole person: chronic cough, poor growth, shortened life expectancy, treated with airway clearance, enzymes, antibiotics and CFTR modulators.

questions.stem: Enterogastric reflex: what stimulates it, what does CCK target, and why is the reflex needed?

questions.stem: What is the hepatic portal system, and what is its benefit?

questions.stem: Eating a fatty meal before drinking alcohol slows intoxication. Explain using where alcohol is absorbed.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old traveler has fever, nausea, diarrhea and jaundice after eating local shellfish. Name the organ affected and the most likely disease. Which two liver cell types does the virus affect? Why is the disease underreported? Name two ways to prevent it.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student develops flu-like illness and yellow eyes weeks after swimming in a lagoon where clothes were washed. Name the disease, explain the yellow eyes, and name one thing she did that could have harmed her liver further.
questions.answer_text: Hepatitis A. Damaged hepatocytes cannot process and excrete bilirubin, which builds up in tissues (jaundice). She treated her fever with acetaminophen, which is toxic to the liver at high doses. There is no specific antiviral; treatment is supportive.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old ex-smoker who drinks daily has weight loss, deep epigastric pain radiating to the back that eases when he leans forward, and greasy stools. CT shows a mass in the tail of the pancreas. Name the diagnosis and three findings that point to the pancreas.
questions.answer_text: Pancreatic cancer. Pain radiating to the back and eased by leaning forward; steatorrhea (no pancreatic lipase); epigastric tenderness; smoking and alcohol as risk factors; imaging. Negative Murphy's sign and normal liver and spleen argue against gallbladder disease.

questions.stem: How would the presentation above differ if the tumor were in the head of the pancreas?
questions.answer_text: It could block the common bile duct, causing painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign).

questions.stem: A newborn in Finland has diarrhea after breastfeeding that stops on soy formula. Name the condition. How does it differ from a milk allergy?
questions.answer_text: Congenital lactase deficiency (primary congenital lactose intolerance). An intolerance is a lack of an enzyme, not an immune reaction; a milk allergy is an immune (often IgE) response to milk proteins.

questions.stem: Name two signs a doctor checks for appendicitis and the surgery used to treat it. What happens if the appendix ruptures?
questions.answer_text: McBurney's point tenderness, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, obturator sign. Appendectomy. Rupture spreads bacteria into the abdomen, causing peritonitis.

questions.stem: A patient has peritonitis after surgery and stays sick despite strong antibiotics. Why would the doctor insert a drainage tube?
questions.answer_text: Pus and infected fluid collect in the peritoneal cavity (an abscess). Antibiotics cannot penetrate an abscess well, so it must be drained.

questions.stem: Explain how obesity can harm the digestive system. Give three mechanisms.
questions.answer_text: Abdominal pressure weakens the lower esophageal sphincter (GERD, hiatal hernia); fatty liver disease; gallstones; visceral fat releases inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α); higher risk of colorectal, esophageal and pancreatic cancer.

questions.stem: What is Barrett's esophagus, what causes it and why is it important?
questions.answer_text: Replacement of the esophagus's stratified squamous lining with simple columnar (intestine-like) cells, caused by long-term acid reflux (GERD). It is a precancerous change that raises the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: Why is lactose intolerance not an allergy? What happens to the undigested lactose?
questions.answer_text: It is a lack of lactase, not an immune response. Lactose reaches the colon, draws water in (osmotic diarrhea) and is fermented by bacteria, producing gas and bloating.

questions.stem: Describe the location of the esophagus from beginning to end.
questions.answer_text: It starts behind the cricoid cartilage (about C6), runs through the posterior mediastinum behind the trachea, passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm and runs a few centimeters in the abdomen before joining the stomach at the cardia.

questions.stem: A patient's stomach acid production is high and he has multiple duodenal ulcers. Tests show a gastrin-secreting tumor. Name the syndrome. Why are ulcers forming in the duodenum?
questions.answer_text: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Excess gastrin drives massive HCl secretion that overwhelms the duodenum's bicarbonate buffering.

questions.stem: Describe protein digestion from mouth to absorption.
questions.answer_text: No protein digestion in the mouth. Stomach: HCl denatures proteins and activates pepsin, which cuts them into polypeptides. Small intestine: pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase cut polypeptides into smaller peptides; brush-border aminopeptidases and dipeptidases make amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides. These are absorbed by sodium-dependent cotransport into enterocytes and enter blood capillaries to the hepatic portal vein.

questions.stem: Describe fat digestion and absorption from mouth to lymph.
questions.answer_text: Lingual and gastric lipases start digestion. In the duodenum, CCK releases bile; bile salts emulsify fat. Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides, which form micelles with bile salts. They diffuse into enterocytes, are rebuilt into triglycerides, packed into chylomicrons and enter lacteals, then lymph and the thoracic duct.

questions.stem: Describe how exercise affects the digestive system in the short term and long term.
questions.answer_text: Short term: sympathetic activity reduces gut blood flow and slows digestion and gastric emptying; intense exercise can cause nausea, cramps, reflux or diarrhea. Long term: regular moderate exercise speeds colon transit (less constipation), helps control weight, improves insulin sensitivity, lowers risk of colon cancer, gallstones, fatty liver and diverticular disease, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

questions.stem: Describe how obesity affects the digestive system. Name at least four conditions linked to it.
questions.answer_text: Higher abdominal pressure and a weaker lower esophageal sphincter cause GERD and hiatal hernia; excess fat in the liver causes fatty liver disease, which can progress to cirrhosis; cholesterol-rich bile causes gallstones; inflammatory cytokines from visceral fat damage tissues; higher risk of colorectal, esophageal adenocarcinoma, pancreatic, liver and gallbladder cancers; altered gut microbiome.

questions.stem: Describe a peptic ulcer at each level: cell, tissue, organ and whole person.
questions.answer_text: Cell: H. pylori or NSAIDs damage epithelial cells and reduce mucus and bicarbonate; acid and pepsin digest exposed cells. Tissue: an erosion deepens through the mucosa into the submucosa or muscle layer. Organ: the stomach or duodenal wall can bleed or perforate. Whole person: burning epigastric pain, nausea, black stools, anemia; treated with PPIs, antibiotics for H. pylori and stopping NSAIDs.

questions.stem: Describe colorectal cancer at each level: cell, tissue, organ and whole person. How is it screened for and prevented?
questions.answer_text: Cell: mutations (often APC, then KRAS and p53) let colon epithelial cells divide uncontrollably. Tissue: an adenomatous polyp grows and becomes an invasive adenocarcinoma. Organ: the tumor narrows the colon, bleeds and can spread to lymph nodes and liver. Whole person: blood in stool, change in bowel habits, anemia, weight loss. Screening: colonoscopy (removing polyps), stool tests. Prevention: fiber-rich diet, less red and processed meat, exercise, no smoking, limited alcohol.

questions.stem: Describe lactose intolerance at the cell, organ and whole-person level.
questions.answer_text: Cell: enterocytes in the small intestine make too little lactase on their brush border. Organ: undigested lactose stays in the lumen, drawing in water (osmotic diarrhea); colon bacteria ferment it, producing gas and acids. Whole person: bloating, cramps, gas and diarrhea 30 minutes to 2 hours after dairy; diagnosed with a hydrogen breath test; managed with lactose-free foods or lactase pills.

questions.stem: Describe hepatitis at the cell, organ and whole-person level.
questions.answer_text: Cell: virus (or alcohol, drugs) infects or injures hepatocytes; immune cells kill infected hepatocytes, releasing ALT and AST. Organ: liver inflammation; chronic hepatitis B or C causes fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver cancer. Whole person: fatigue, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, right upper abdominal pain; prevented by vaccines (A, B), safe food and water, and avoiding shared needles.

questions.stem: Describe appendicitis from cause to treatment.
questions.answer_text: A fecalith or swollen lymphoid tissue blocks the appendix. Mucus and bacteria build up, pressure rises, blood flow falls and the wall becomes inflamed and can die (gangrene) and rupture. Pain starts near the navel (visceral) and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney's point) as the peritoneum is irritated; fever, nausea and high white count follow. Treatment: appendectomy (or antibiotics in selected cases); rupture causes peritonitis.

questions.stem: Describe diarrhea at the cell and whole-person level, and compare osmotic, secretory and exudative types.
questions.answer_text: Cells either absorb too little water (osmotic: unabsorbed solutes such as lactose), secrete too much Cl− and water (secretory: cholera, E. coli toxins) or are damaged and leak blood and pus (exudative: Shigella, ulcerative colitis). Whole person: frequent loose stools, dehydration, loss of Na+, K+ and HCO3−, metabolic acidosis; treated with oral rehydration solution and by treating the cause.

questions.explanation: through lacteals.

questions.stem: Mast cells secrete serotonin.
questions.explanation: in humans mostly histamine, but mast cells can also release serotonin.

questions.stem: Basophils and eosinophils are major phagocytes.
questions.explanation: their main role is releasing chemicals; phagocytosis is limited.

questions.stem: Innate immunity remembers each pathogen and responds faster the second time.
questions.explanation: memory belongs to adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: Helper T cells recognize antigen on MHC I.
questions.explanation: they recognize antigen on MHC II.

questions.stem: T-cell receptors only recognize antigens presented on MHC.
Xenografts come from a genetically different member of the same species.
questions.explanation: that is an allograft; a xenograft comes from another species.

questions.stem: The earliest thymocytes express neither CD4 nor CD8.
questions.explanation: they are "double negative," then become "double positive" before choosing one.

questions.stem: Saliva does not contain IgA.
Pleiotropy (one cytokine having many effects) is a property of cytokines.
Skin is part of the innate immune system's first line of defense.
The thymus is most active before puberty.
Lymph nodes filter blood and the spleen filters lymph.
questions.explanation: lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood.

questions.stem: Toll-like receptors are found on B cells and T cells only.
questions.explanation: they are found mainly on innate cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells (and on many other cells).

questions.stem: The complement system can kill bacteria by punching holes in their membranes.
questions.explanation: through the membrane attack complex.

questions.stem: A person must be exposed to an allergen at least once before having an allergic reaction to it.
questions.explanation: the first exposure sensitizes them.

questions.stem: Urticaria is always caused by an allergy.
questions.explanation: hives can also come from cold, pressure, exercise, infections or unknown causes.

questions.stem: CVID is usually diagnosed in infancy.
questions.explanation: usually in teens or adults (ages 20–40 is common).

questions.stem: SCID is often called "bubble boy" disease.
HIV can be spread by mosquitoes.
Multiple sclerosis affects the peripheral nervous system.
questions.explanation: it affects the CNS (brain, spinal cord, optic nerves).

questions.stem: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the United States.
Serum sickness is a type IV hypersensitivity.
questions.explanation: it is type III.

questions.stem: The primary lymphoid organs are the ______ and ______. Name one secondary lymphoid organ.
questions.answer_text: red bone marrow and thymus; lymph node, spleen, tonsils, Peyer's patches or appendix

questions.stem: List the five white blood cells from most to least abundant.
questions.answer_text: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils ("Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas")

questions.stem: Helper T cells carry the surface protein ______; cytotoxic T cells carry ______.
MHC class I is on ______ and presents to ______ T cells. MHC class II is on ______ and presents to ______ T cells.
questions.answer_text: all nucleated cells, CD8 (cytotoxic); antigen-presenting cells, CD4 (helper)

questions.stem: Cytotoxic T cells kill by releasing ______ and ______.
An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive baby makes anti-Rh antibodies of class ______. This can cause ______ in a later pregnancy. It is prevented with ______.
questions.answer_text: IgG; hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis); RhoGAM (anti-D immunoglobulin)

questions.stem: The five cardinal signs of inflammation in Latin are rubor, calor, tumor, dolor and functio laesa. Give each in English.
questions.answer_text: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function

questions.stem: Name the four steps of phagocyte mobilization in order.
The two main antimicrobial proteins of innate defense are ______ and ______.
MALT stands for ______.
The lymphoid follicles in the wall of the ileum are called ______.
Waldeyer's ring consists of the ______, ______, ______ and ______ tonsils.
Class I MHC proteins are on almost all body cells except ______.
Antibodies are made of two ______ chains and two ______ chains.
Pieces of an antigen that an antibody or receptor binds are called ______.
B cells activated in a primary response become either ______ cells or memory B cells.
______ highlight molecules to be phagocytosed by binding receptors on phagocytes.
______ is the breakdown of a cell caused by damage to its plasma membrane.
Lymph is derived from ______ fluid and carries bacteria to lymph nodes, where they are destroyed by ______.
The red pulp of the spleen contains red blood cells, ______ and ______.
Collectins, ficolins and pentraxins act as pattern recognition receptors and activate complement through the ______ or ______ pathway.
Phagocytes release two kinds of signaling molecules: ______ and ______.
Interleukin-1, made by macrophages, promotes helper T-cell proliferation and causes ______.
A blood marker of inflammation made by the liver is C-______ protein.
The rare disease in which a baby is born with very few or no functional T cells and B cells is ______ (initials).
Name the organs of the immune system listed in the rules and one function of each: bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, skin.
questions.answer_text: Bone marrow: makes all blood cells; B-cell maturation. Thymus: T-cell maturation and selection. Spleen: filters blood, removes old red cells, mounts responses to blood-borne antigens. Lymph nodes: filter lymph; B and T cells meet antigen. Skin: physical and chemical barrier; Langerhans cells capture antigens.

questions.stem: The three complement activation pathways are the ______, ______ and ______ pathways.
Name three anatomical or physical barriers of innate immunity.
questions.answer_text: any three: skin, mucous membranes, mucus, cilia (mucociliary escalator), vibrissae, tears, saliva, stomach acid, tight junctions, normal microbiota

questions.stem: Name four innate immune cells.
questions.answer_text: any four: neutrophils, macrophages/monocytes, dendritic cells, NK cells, eosinophils, basophils, mast cells

In myasthenia gravis, drooping eyelids are called ______ and the drugs that boost acetylcholine are acetylcholinesterase ______.
The treatment for CVID and other antibody deficiencies is replacement with ______ (abbreviation).
Match each graft type.
match_choices: Genetically different person of the same species

Acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Gluten triggers damage to intestinal villi

Kills parasitic worms; role in allergy
Kills tumor and virus-infected cells without prior sensitization

Dimer in saliva, tears, milk and intestinal juice

match_choices: Fatty acids made from arachidonic acid
Granules of mast cells and basophils

Promotes Th2 cells and switching to IgE
Turns down immune responses; inhibits macrophages

questions.stem: For each item, write the line of defense it belongs to (1st, 2nd or 3rd): a) skin  b) plasma cell  c) neutrophil  d) lysozyme in tears  e) inflammation  f) antibodies  g) helper T cell  h) normal microbiota
questions.answer_text: a) 1st  b) 3rd  c) 2nd  d) 1st  e) 2nd  f) 3rd  g) 3rd  h) 1st

questions.stem: Classify each as active or passive, and natural or artificial: a) infection with a pathogen  b) antibodies passed from mother to fetus  c) injection of gamma globulin  d) injection of an attenuated (weakened) pathogen
questions.answer_text: a) natural active  b) natural passive  c) artificial passive  d) artificial active

questions.stem: Match the hypersensitivity type to its example.
match_choices: Poison ivy rash the next day

questions.stem: Identify the disorder: a) Women who are or recently were pregnant are at higher risk.  b) Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies are present.  c) Four courses include relapsing-remitting and primary progressive.  d) Treated with antiretrovirals and reverse transcriptase inhibitors.  e) Baby born without a thymus and with low calcium.
questions.answer_text: a) Graves' disease  b) rheumatoid arthritis  c) multiple sclerosis  d) HIV/AIDS  e) DiGeorge syndrome

Match the immunodeficiency to its description.

Low antibodies, poor vaccine response; often diagnosed in adults
Absent or nonfunctional T and B cells from birth
Missing thymus and parathyroids; low T cells and low calcium
No mature B cells; BTK mutation; boys

questions.stem: Match each toll-like receptor to what it recognizes.
Two children have frequent infections. Use their blood results to answer.
after_text: a) What type of immunodeficiency does each child most likely have? b) Tuesday has normal B-cell numbers. Give one reason his antibodies are still low. c) For each treatment write W, T, both (B) or neither (N): IVIG, bone marrow transplant, antibiotics, gene therapy.
questions.answer_text: a) Wednesday: antibody (humoral) deficiency such as CVID — Ig low, cell counts normal. Tuesday: SCID (T−, B+, NK− pattern, e.g., X-linked common gamma chain defect). b) B cells need helper T-cell signals (cytokines, CD40L) to class-switch and become plasma cells. c) IVIG – B; bone marrow transplant – T; antibiotics – B; gene therapy – T.
questions.explanation: Ig low, cell counts normal. Tuesday: SCID (T−, B+, NK− pattern, e.g., X-linked common gamma chain defect). b) B cells need helper T-cell signals (cytokines, CD40L) to class-switch and become plasma cells. c) IVIG – B; bone marrow transplant – T; antibiotics – B; gene therapy – T.

questions.stem: Wednesday has septic shock and a nurse has anaphylactic shock. For each treatment write W, N (nurse), B (both) or NA (neither): IV fluids, antibiotics, steroids, antihistamines, epinephrine.
questions.answer_text: IV fluids – B; antibiotics – W; steroids – B; antihistamines – N; epinephrine – B (norepinephrine is preferred in septic shock).

questions.stem: Each person inherits one HLA haplotype from each parent. What is the chance that two siblings are HLA-identical? What is the chance that at least one of two siblings matches a patient?
A blood smear shows 70% neutrophils with many band (immature) forms. What does this suggest? What would a smear with 15% eosinophils suggest?
questions.answer_text: Neutrophilia with a "left shift": acute bacterial infection. Eosinophilia: parasitic worm infection or allergy/asthma.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl has a CD4 count of 89 cells/µL, recurrent pneumonia, tuberculosis, chronic diarrhea and severe anemia. Name the disease. Why does she keep getting pneumonia? Name one class of drugs used to treat her.
questions.answer_text: AIDS (advanced HIV infection; CD4 < 200). Without helper T cells, she cannot activate B cells, cytotoxic T cells and macrophages, so opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia take hold. Drug classes: nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non-nucleoside RT inhibitors, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, fusion/entry inhibitors.

questions.stem: Give three differences between innate and adaptive immunity.
questions.answer_text: Innate: present from birth, nonspecific, acts in minutes to hours, no memory, germline-encoded receptors (PRRs). Adaptive: acquired, specific to one antigen, takes days the first time, has memory, receptors made by gene rearrangement.

questions.stem: Name the cardinal signs of inflammation and explain how histamine produces two of them.
questions.answer_text: Redness, heat, swelling, pain (and loss of function). Histamine dilates arterioles (redness, heat) and makes capillaries leaky, so fluid enters tissue (swelling) and presses on nerves (pain).

questions.stem: Give one reason a high fever helps and one reason it can harm.
questions.answer_text: Helps: slows microbial growth, the liver and spleen hold back iron and zinc, speeds repair and immune activity. Harms: very high fever denatures proteins, can cause seizures and dehydration, and raises heart rate and O2 demand.

questions.stem: Name five ways antibodies inactivate antigens.
questions.answer_text: Neutralization, agglutination, precipitation, complement activation (fixation), opsonization (also antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity).

questions.stem: Complete the table of hypersensitivity types.
questions.answer_text: I (immediate): IgE on mast cells and basophils, histamine — anaphylaxis, hay fever, asthma. II (cytotoxic): IgG/IgM against cell-surface antigens, complement — transfusion reaction, HDN, Graves', myasthenia gravis. III (immune complex): antigen–antibody complexes deposited in tissue — serum sickness, lupus, Arthus reaction. IV (delayed): T cells and macrophages — contact dermatitis, TB skin test, transplant rejection.
questions.explanation: anaphylaxis, hay fever, asthma. II (cytotoxic): IgG/IgM against cell-surface antigens, complement — transfusion reaction, HDN, Graves', myasthenia gravis. III (immune complex): antigen–antibody complexes deposited in tissue — serum sickness, lupus, Arthus reaction. IV (delayed): T cells and macrophages — contact dermatitis, TB skin test, transplant rejection.

questions.stem: Why can a bone marrow transplant from an identical twin be given with little risk of rejection?
questions.answer_text: An identical twin has the same MHC (HLA) proteins, so the cells are recognized as self; there is little rejection or graft-versus-host disease.

questions.stem: Cancer cells are "self." How can the immune system still recognize them? Use the terms MHC I and neoantigen, and name two cells that kill them.
questions.answer_text: Mutated proteins are broken down and their fragments (neoantigens) are shown on MHC I, where cytotoxic T cells recognize them as nonself. Cancer cells that hide by lowering MHC I are killed by NK cells. Cells: CD8 cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.

questions.stem: Describe T-cell development in the thymus, including positive and negative selection.
questions.answer_text: Precursors from bone marrow enter the thymus and build T-cell receptors (double negative → double positive CD4+CD8+). Positive selection (cortex): cells that bind self-MHC weakly survive; those that cannot bind die. Cells become CD4 (MHC II) or CD8 (MHC I) single positive. Negative selection (medulla): cells that bind self-antigen too strongly undergo apoptosis, creating self-tolerance. Survivors leave as naive T cells.

questions.stem: How does a B cell switch from making IgM to IgG or IgE?
questions.answer_text: Class switching: helper T cells give signals (CD40L and cytokines such as IL-4 for IgE) that make the B cell recombine its DNA, swapping the heavy-chain constant region while keeping the same variable region and specificity.

questions.stem: Name the four kinds of acquired immunity with one example each.
questions.answer_text: Natural active – recovering from chickenpox. Artificial active – a vaccine. Natural passive – maternal IgG across the placenta or IgA in breast milk. Artificial passive – antivenom or IVIG.

questions.stem: Describe the complement cascade and its three main outcomes.
questions.answer_text: Complement proteins circulate inactive and are activated in a cascade by the classical (antibody), lectin or alternative (microbial surface) pathway, all converging on cleavage of C3. Outcomes: opsonization (C3b), inflammation and chemotaxis (C3a, C5a), and lysis by the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9).

questions.stem: Why do complement proteins circulate in an inactive (pro-) form?
questions.answer_text: They are powerful inducers of inflammation and cell lysis; keeping them inactive until a pathogen is detected protects the body's own cells.

questions.stem: How does the innate immune system recognize pathogens?
questions.answer_text: Pattern recognition receptors (such as toll-like receptors) bind pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) shared by broad classes of microbes, such as LPS, flagellin and viral double-stranded RNA.

questions.stem: AIDS: what type of pathogen causes it? Describe its effect on weight, lymph nodes and body temperature. Can people with HIV live long lives today?
questions.answer_text: A retrovirus (HIV). Weight loss (wasting), swollen lymph nodes and recurring fevers. Yes — antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus so people can live near-normal lifespans.
questions.explanation: antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus so people can live near-normal lifespans.

questions.stem: Explain how HIV replicates and give two drug targets.
questions.answer_text: HIV gp120 binds CD4 and a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4); gp41 fuses the membranes; reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA; integrase inserts it into host DNA; new proteins are cut by protease and virions bud off. Drug targets: entry/fusion, reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has constipation, fatigue, weight gain, dry skin and a lump in her neck. Name the disease, the antibodies elevated, the hormone results and one treatment.
questions.answer_text: Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies. High TSH, low T3 and T4. Levothyroxine.

questions.stem: Clara, 33, has had mononucleosis and now has dizziness, arm weakness and tingling, and partial loss of vision in one eye. MRI shows white-matter lesions. Name the disease and give four supporting reasons. How is it treated? Can it be cured?
questions.answer_text: Multiple sclerosis: neurological symptoms in different places at different times; optic neuritis (vision loss); MRI lesions in CNS white matter (demyelination); young woman; prior Epstein-Barr virus (mono) is a known risk factor; oligoclonal bands in cerebrospinal fluid. Treatment: corticosteroids for flares, disease-modifying drugs (interferon beta, monoclonal antibodies), physical therapy. No cure.

questions.stem: Jonny, a pianist, has stiff, painful, red, warm, swollen finger and wrist joints, a high sedimentation rate and abnormal antibodies. Name the disease. What is happening in the joints? Would neutrophils in his joint fluid be normal, high or low? Can he be cured? Name one long-term treatment.
questions.answer_text: Rheumatoid arthritis. The immune system attacks the synovial membrane, which thickens (pannus) and erodes cartilage and bone. High — neutrophils flood inflamed joints. No cure. DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate), biologics (TNF inhibitors), NSAIDs, low-dose steroids, physical therapy.
questions.explanation: neutrophils flood inflamed joints. No cure. DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate), biologics (TNF inhibitors), NSAIDs, low-dose steroids, physical therapy.

questions.stem: A boy has a red facial rash, fever, painful joints, hair loss and swollen lymph nodes. Name the disease and give two treatments. Should he keep playing soccer outdoors?
questions.answer_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydroxychloroquine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants. He can stay active (exercise helps) but must use strong sun protection and rest during flares.

questions.stem: A patient has an anaphylactic reaction. Explain what happens in the body, the blood test that confirms it, and how epinephrine helps.
questions.answer_text: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, which release histamine and other mediators: vasodilation drops blood pressure, leaky vessels cause swelling, bronchi constrict. Serum tryptase confirms mast-cell activation. Epinephrine constricts blood vessels (raises pressure) and relaxes airway smooth muscle.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a food allergy and a food intolerance?
questions.answer_text: An allergy is an immune (often IgE) response to a food protein. An intolerance does not involve the immune system, such as lactose intolerance caused by missing lactase.

questions.stem: Transplant patients: Patient 3's graft clots within minutes; Patient 4 has reduced kidney function and flu-like symptoms 2 months after transplant; Patient 5's liver loses bile ducts over years. What condition do they share, why does it occur, and what is each type called?
questions.answer_text: Transplant rejection: the recipient's immune system recognizes donor HLA as foreign. Patient 3: hyperacute (pre-existing antibodies; remove graft). Patient 4: acute (T-cell mediated; treat with higher-dose immunosuppressants and steroids). Patient 5: chronic rejection.

questions.stem: Why does an Rh-negative mother usually not harm her first Rh-positive baby?
questions.answer_text: She is only sensitized at delivery when fetal blood enters her circulation. Her first antibodies are IgM, which cannot cross the placenta; IgG made in later pregnancies does cross it.

questions.stem: Explain why someone who had chickenpox as a child usually does not get it again.
questions.answer_text: Memory B and T cells made in the first infection respond quickly and strongly on re-exposure (secondary response), producing high levels of IgG before the virus can cause disease.

questions.stem: Why does a person with HIV become susceptible to infections that would not harm a healthy person?
questions.answer_text: HIV destroys CD4 helper T cells, which activate B cells, cytotoxic T cells and macrophages. With few helper cells, both antibody and cell-mediated responses fail, so opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, TB, candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma) take hold.

questions.stem: Explain how the thymus changes with age and why.
questions.answer_text: It is large in children and shrinks after puberty, with lymphoid tissue replaced by fat (thymic involution), as part of immune aging and influenced by sex hormones and steroids. Fewer new T cells are made, but existing memory T cells persist.

questions.stem: Describe the sequence of events in an allergic reaction from first exposure to symptoms.
questions.answer_text: Sensitization: an allergen is taken up by APCs and shown to Th2 cells; IL-4 drives B cells to make IgE, which binds Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils. Re-exposure: the allergen cross-links bound IgE, triggering degranulation. Histamine, leukotrienes and prostaglandins cause vasodilation, leaky vessels, smooth-muscle contraction, mucus and itching within minutes. A late phase hours later brings eosinophils and more inflammation.

questions.stem: Describe the primary immune response to a new bacterial infection, from entry to antibody production.
questions.answer_text: Barriers are breached; complement and neutrophils/macrophages respond (inflammation). Dendritic cells capture antigen, travel to a lymph node and present it on MHC II to helper T cells. Helper T cells activate B cells specific to the antigen (CD40L, cytokines). B cells proliferate (clonal selection), class-switch and become plasma cells making antibodies (IgM first, then IgG) and memory cells. Antibodies neutralize, opsonize and activate complement. Peak about 10–14 days.

questions.stem: Compare humoral and cell-mediated immunity.
questions.answer_text: Humoral: B cells and antibodies in body fluids; targets extracellular pathogens and toxins; antigens recognized directly. Cell-mediated: T cells; CD8 cells kill infected or cancer cells, CD4 cells direct the response; antigen recognized only on MHC; key in viral infections, cancer and transplant rejection.

questions.stem: Describe the four steps of acute inflammation and its purpose.
questions.answer_text: Injury or infection triggers mast cells and macrophages to release histamine, cytokines and other mediators. Vasodilation and increased permeability bring fluid, proteins and clotting factors (redness, heat, swelling, pain). Phagocytes are mobilized (margination, diapedesis, chemotaxis) and destroy microbes. Repair follows. Purpose: contain and destroy pathogens, remove debris and begin healing.

questions.stem: Explain how toll-like receptors link innate and adaptive immunity.
questions.answer_text: TLRs on dendritic cells and macrophages detect PAMPs, activating NF-κB and the release of cytokines. This makes dendritic cells mature, display more MHC and co-stimulatory molecules (B7) and travel to lymph nodes, where they activate naive T cells, starting the adaptive response.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has had repeated sinus infections, pneumonia and diarrhea for years. Tests show low IgG and IgA, normal B-cell numbers and a poor response to the tetanus vaccine. Name the disorder, explain the defect, and give its treatment.
questions.answer_text: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). B cells are present but fail to mature into plasma cells and make antibodies, so the person cannot clear encapsulated bacteria. Treatment: lifelong IVIG or subcutaneous immunoglobulin, and antibiotics for infections.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has thrush, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive and Pneumocystis pneumonia. He has very few T cells. Name the disorder, explain why both T and B immunity fail, and give two treatments.
questions.answer_text: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Without functional T cells, B cells cannot be activated, so both cell-mediated and antibody immunity fail. Treatment: bone marrow (stem cell) transplant, gene therapy, enzyme replacement (for ADA-SCID), IVIG; avoid live vaccines.

questions.stem: Describe the stages of HIV infection and how it is diagnosed.
questions.answer_text: Acute infection (2–4 weeks): flu-like illness, high viral load. Clinical latency: few symptoms for years while CD4 counts fall slowly. AIDS: CD4 below 200 cells/µL or an AIDS-defining illness (Pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi sarcoma, TB). Diagnosed with antigen/antibody tests (p24 antigen and anti-HIV antibodies), confirmed with viral load testing.

questions.stem: Compare rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis: target, cells involved, symptoms and treatment.
questions.answer_text: RA: synovial joint lining; T cells, B cells (rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP), macrophages; symmetric painful, swollen joints with morning stiffness; DMARDs (methotrexate), biologics (TNF inhibitors), steroids, NSAIDs. MS: CNS myelin; autoreactive T cells, B cells, macrophages; vision loss, numbness, weakness, balance problems in flares; steroids for flares, disease-modifying drugs (interferon beta, anti-CD20 antibodies).

questions.stem: Compare Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
questions.answer_text: Graves': antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor; hyperthyroid (weight loss, heat intolerance, fast heart rate, bulging eyes, goiter); low TSH, high T3/T4; treated with antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine or surgery. Hashimoto's: T cells and anti-TPO/thyroglobulin antibodies destroy the gland; hypothyroid (weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin); high TSH, low T4; treated with levothyroxine.

questions.stem: A teacher has drooping eyelids and double vision by the end of each school day, and her arm tires when writing on the board. Name the disorder and explain the mechanism. What test and treatment are used?
questions.answer_text: Myasthenia gravis: antibodies block and destroy acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction (type II), so repeated stimulation weakens contraction. Test: anti-AChR antibodies (also the ice-pack or edrophonium test, EMG). Treatment: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppressants, thymectomy, IVIG or plasmapheresis for crises.

questions.stem: A child gets a tetanus booster and 8 hours later has a painful, red, swollen area at the injection site. A week after receiving a drug made from animal serum, another patient develops fever, rash and joint pain. Name each reaction, its type and its mechanism.
questions.answer_text: First: Arthus reaction (type III, local) — high antibody levels form immune complexes with the antigen in local vessel walls, activating complement and neutrophils. Second: serum sickness (type III, systemic) — antibodies to foreign proteins form complexes that deposit in joints, skin and kidneys.
questions.explanation: high antibody levels form immune complexes with the antigen in local vessel walls, activating complement and neutrophils. Second: serum sickness (type III, systemic) — antibodies to foreign proteins form complexes that deposit in joints, skin and kidneys.

questions.stem: A gardener develops an itchy, blistering rash two days after handling poison ivy. Name the condition, its hypersensitivity type and why it takes days to appear.
questions.answer_text: Allergic contact dermatitis, type IV (delayed). Urushiol acts as a hapten; sensitized T cells must be recruited to the skin and release cytokines that attract macrophages, which takes 24–72 hours.

questions.stem: What is the difference between urticaria and anaphylaxis?
questions.answer_text: Urticaria is a local skin reaction (itchy hives) from mast-cell histamine. Anaphylaxis is a severe, systemic type I reaction involving two or more body systems (skin, airway, circulation, gut), with airway swelling and low blood pressure; it can kill within minutes and needs epinephrine.
